claim: Regret of any consistent bandit policy grows at least logarithmically with the number of pulls, and UCB1 and Thompson sampling reach that rate; the guarantees are asymptotic and the constants are silent at tens of pulls.
agent_test: Framing only. Check empirically that per-trial regret flattens after about 30 pulls in replayed operator logs.

claim: Thompson sampling with Beta(1,1) priors is asymptotically optimal on Bernoulli arms (Kaufmann et al.); the first finite-time proof (Agrawal and Goyal) is weaker (gap dependence 1/Delta^3).
agent_test: Implement Beta-Bernoulli TS over operators; compare regret with UCB1 on logged operator outcomes.

claim: In simulation with thousands of pulls, Thompson sampling matches or beats UCB variants, has no tuning parameter, and tolerates delayed feedback better (UCB/TS regret ratio 2.65 at delay 1 to 3.82 at delay 1000; re-checked against the Chapelle and Li table).
agent_test: Our feedback arrives only after a branch is scored (delay). Simulate delay in a replay of operator logs.

claim: Tuned simple heuristics (epsilon-greedy, Boltzmann) can beat UCB1 in 1000-step simulations when tuned per setting; the hidden cost of any bandit is tuning.
agent_test: Compare untuned defaults, not tuned ones; report sensitivity to one exploration constant.

claim: When the best operator changes, plain stationary bandits lag; sliding-window, discounted or restart variants recover, with total regret of order sqrt(T times the number of breakpoints times log T) (and a sqrt(T) lower bound in a two-breakpoint game), and need a window or discount that depends on the unknown number of changes. Own simulation (not a published source): count caps of 5 to 50 changed regret by at most about 0.15 at 30 to 60 pulls, even after a mid-run switch.
agent_test: Replay logs where operator value shifts with search state; compare plain, window 10/20/40 and restart.
audit_note: Garivier and Moulines give total regret O(sqrt(T Upsilon_T log T)) for Upsilon_T breakpoints and a sqrt(T) lower bound for a two-breakpoint game, not a cost of order sqrt(T) per change; the own-simulation count-cap effect is at most 0.15 (12.54 vs 12.69), not under 0.15, and cannot be checked against a source.
claim_before_audit: When the best operator changes, plain stationary bandits lag; sliding-window, discounted or restart variants recover, at a cost of order sqrt(T) per change, and need a window or threshold that depends on unknown change counts. Gap search: every windowed or discounted Thompson study opened runs 200 to 50,000 pulls, and my 30 to 60 pull simulation shows count caps of 5 to 50 change regret by under 0.15, even after a mid-run switch.

claim: In short adaptive-operator-selection tests (5 operators, epochs of 50 or 200 pulls) bandits beat Probability Matching and Adaptive Pursuit, but the change detector adds nothing for 50-pull epochs or Boolean rewards, and rare large rewards leave every method near random.
agent_test: Use the da Costa scenarios as a unit test of our selector at 50 and 200 steps.

claim: The Thierens Probability Matching and Adaptive Pursuit setup only partly replicates: best p_min was 0 to 0.01, not 0.1, and PM and AP did not differ in two of three scenarios.
agent_test: None; caution on inherited default parameters only.

claim: Credit assignment matters more than selection rule: crediting operators by lineage survival over several generations beat crediting immediate fitness gain, but the benefit decays after a few steps.
agent_test: Credit an operator for the 2-3 step descendants of its output, not only the immediate score; compare at equal tokens.

claim: Dynamic Thompson sampling (capped Beta counts, C=100) is reported to beat a UCB sliding-window selector (FRRMAB) in 16 of 19 IGD and 18 of 19 HV comparisons in MOEA/D; the text and the IGD table disagree on UF8, the authors chose the benchmarks, and it is a preprint.
agent_test: Test capped-count TS against plain TS on non-stationary replay.

claim: In LLM prompt optimisation, adding strategy selection raises accuracy (OPTS, Llama-3-8B, 27 BBH tasks, 3 seeds: 48.43 plain, 53.87 uniform choice, 55.67 Thompson), but most of the gain comes from having the options. Thompson over uniform is +1.8 points with per-task SD of several points, and only +0.59 with the GA optimiser (Table 10). Gap search: paired over the 27 tasks, the DE gap (+1.79) is significant (t=2.61, sign test 18-7, Wilcoxon p=0.008) but the GA gap (+0.60) is not (t=0.96, 12 wins vs 14 losses).
agent_test: Ablate: fixed operator vs uniform random operator vs TS at equal tokens; report the TS minus uniform gap over many seeds.

claim: Letting the LLM choose its own strategy does worse than the bandit: OPTS(APET) 52.87 vs uniform 53.87 vs TS 55.67, and Meta-Reasoner's direct-LLM-choice ablation scored 82 vs 89 (Game of 24) and 80.74 vs 84.13 (TheoremQA). Both papers are authors' own ablations and Meta-Reasoner's text has internal inconsistencies.
agent_test: Compare LLM-picks-operator vs UCB/TS vs uniform at equal tokens.

claim: Best-arm-identification rules (sequential halving, continuous rejection) beat uniform and vanilla UCB for choosing among candidate prompts under a small fixed evaluation budget (5 evaluations per prompt: +12 to +16 percent over uniform, +3 to +7 over UCB); the edge vanishes at about 30 evaluations per prompt. Gap search: in my i.i.d. simulation at about 5 evaluations per candidate, halving ties tuned UCB and Thompson within 0.03 to 0.04 in P(best) and beats plain UCB1 only when candidates are many (30).
agent_test: Use successive halving, not UCB, to choose among final candidates at about 5 evaluations each.

claim: Pryzant et al. found UCB at least as good as successive rejects and halving for prompt selection while TRIPLE found BAI rules better; differences are 0.01 to 0.04 and probably inside noise.
agent_test: Run both on our candidate sets at equal calls.

claim: When candidates outnumber the budget, sharing information across similar candidates (embeddings, clustering) beat independent-arm baselines in TRIPLE (e.g. 21%/28% over BO-EI on GPT-3.5, with different margins on Llama2), and TS that models shared structure beats independent TS in a shortest-path tutorial; the advantage shrinks as budget grows, and it is untested here how much depends on embedding quality.
agent_test: Treat operators as arms with shared features (task type, search state) rather than independent arms.
audit_note: Numbers and the 'beats independent arms when candidates outnumber budget' finding check out, and gains differ between GPT-3.5 and Llama2, but neither source tests how the gain depends on embedding prediction quality; that part is inference.
claim_before_audit: When candidates outnumber the budget, sharing information across similar candidates (embeddings, clustering) beats independent arms; the gain depends on the embedding predicting quality and differs between models.

claim: Operator value depends on state: no single operator is best through a run, and value falls as parent fitness rises; newer LLM search systems key operator weights on search state. Gap search: Deliberate Evolution's hand-built 4-state weight table beats uniform operator sampling by about 23x in NMSE, but no source compares a state-keyed bandit with a global one, and contextual Thompson guarantees (d^1.5 sqrt(T)) are vacuous at 30 pulls.
agent_test: Log operator gain per state S0-S9 and test whether state-keyed Thompson sampling beats state-free.

claim: In LLM-driven evolutionary search, bandit operator selection gives a small or unmeasured gain over random or uniform: LLaMEA UCB 0.8453 vs random 0.8304 (N=6, SD 0.015 to 0.03); ShinkaEvolve caption says slight and text says significant; TIDE without UCB is best of the ablations at size 50 and worst at size 200.
agent_test: Expect small gains; beat a uniform-random baseline before adding a learner.
audit_note: Minor: the TIDE ablation pattern (w/o UCB best at scale 50, worst at 200) holds on TSP only, and the full TIDE model beats every ablation, so the UCB contribution there is not small at scale 200.

claim: Larger gains in LLM search systems come from stall-triggered changes or meta-guidance than from the bandit (AdaEvolve circle packing: no meta-guidance -0.108 vs no UCB island selection -0.011; Deliberate Evolution: removing the stagnation monitor 15.91 to 13.64 percent accuracy, about 2 problems). Gap search: the claim is now contested. Deliberate Evolution's ablation (operator policy unknown run count) shows removing the stagnation monitor costs 1.8x in NMSE while replacing the state-keyed policy with uniform costs 23x. AdaEvolve's meta-guidance is a prompt directive, not a plain operator switch.
agent_test: Test a stall detector that forces an operator switch versus bandit selection alone.

claim: Small sliding windows forget too fast: SW-UCB with the largest window (SW-UCB-L, 0.8235) is below random in LLaMEA, and small windows drift toward uniform selection; theory puts the window near sqrt(T ln T).
agent_test: If a window is used keep it near sqrt(T ln T); never below about 30 pulls.

claim: Wider-or-deeper Thompson branching (AB-MCTS) beats repeated sampling on mean rank at 128 generations (2.3 vs 3.5), but repeated sampling wins on ARC-AGI at 128 (15.0 vs 12.3 Pass@2) and AB-MCTS only overtakes at 200 to 500 generations. Re-checked against Table 1.
agent_test: On ARC items, compare plain repeated sampling vs a TS go-wide/go-deeper rule at budgets under 128.

claim: LLMs used as bandit agents mostly fail to explore in context (in Krishnamurthy et al., GPT-4 with a basic prompt had suffix failure in more than 60% of replicates; only GPT-4 with chain of thought and externally summarised statistics worked among the prompt designs tested), are biased by arm labels (Semantic Bandits), and numeric contextual bandits on text embeddings often match or beat LLM agents (Berdica et al.); other remedies such as reasoning models or algorithm-guided prompts and fine-tuning also improve exploration.
agent_test: Keep operator selection in code with counts and means, not in the model's free-text judgment.
audit_note: Krishnamurthy et al. found only one satisfactory configuration among GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 prompt designs (GPT-4, chain of thought, summarised statistics), but later sources in the same list show other fixes (algorithm-guided values and fine-tuning in EVOLvE, reasoning models in Zhang et al.), so 'only' is too wide.
claim_before_audit: LLMs used as bandit agents mostly fail to explore in context (suffix failure above 60 percent for basic GPT-4 prompts, T=500) and are biased by arm labels; only chain of thought with summarised statistics works, and numeric bandits on embeddings often match LLM bandits.

claim: Reported gains in the LLM bandit literature rest on few seeds (3 for OPTS, AdaEvolve, TIDE; 6 for LLaMEA), no significance tests, and weak or author-tuned baselines; headline numbers like 50 percent come from near-zero baselines (OPTS task 8: 2.67 to 52.33). Gap search: a task-level paired test is possible from OPTS tables and gives mixed results (DE significant, GA not).
agent_test: Our tests need at least 10 seeds or paired items and a stated minimum effect.
audit_note: Own paired analysis reproduced from OPTS Table 2 (DE: +1.79, t=2.61, TS higher on 18 of 27); 'weak or author-tuned baselines' is only loosely supported (Meta-Reasoner baselines mixed).

claim: OPTS Thompson-over-uniform gap is optimiser dependent. Paired over 27 BBH tasks, DE: +1.79 points, t=2.61 (p about 0.015), TS wins on 18 tasks and loses on 7, Wilcoxon p=0.008. GA: +0.60, t=0.96, TS wins 12 and loses 14, sign test p=0.85. Seeds were averaged (3), so this is across-task evidence only, with equal iteration budgets, not equal API calls.
agent_test: Always run a uniform-choice control; require a paired test over at least 10 items before keeping the bandit.

claim: Credit rules compared head to head with bandit selectors (not Thompson): extreme credit (max of last 10 gains) beat average credit in the Fialho group's tests (racing kept only extreme windows on 22 SAT instances; dynamic MAB with extreme reward was best at every epoch length 50 to 2000), but extreme credit makes bandits favour high-variance operators, helps most at long epochs, and rank-based credit (AUC, sum of ranks) is more robust to reward scale. No head-to-head with Thompson sampling or delayed lineage credit exists.
agent_test: On logged operator results, replay binary, relative, max-of-last-5 and rank credit under the same Thompson rule and compare cumulative reward.

claim: Own simulation (8 operators, 20 to 60 pulls, Bernoulli, 3000 runs): flat-prior Thompson sampling cuts regret versus uniform by only 6 to 13 percent in a hard design and 14 to 33 percent in a typical one; UCB1 (c=sqrt2) by 4 to 18 percent; epsilon-greedy 0.1 and UCB with c=0.5 often beat flat Thompson; a fixed best-guess operator that is right 30 percent of the time beats all learners with flat priors at 8 arms (hard, T=60 regret 5.73 vs TS 6.88 vs uniform 7.90). Synthetic, not real operator logs.
agent_test: Replay real operator logs at 20, 40, 60 pulls: compare Thompson with a weak prior, UCB1, uniform and a fixed best-guess operator.

claim: A wrong prior hurts little at 30 pulls while a right one helps. Theory: loss from a misspecified prior is at most 2 H^2 TV B (tight in worst case, loose for small H). Meta-Thompson tests show no catastrophic failure under 3x too wide or too narrow meta-priors at horizon 200. My simulation (8 operators, T=30): a prior of strength 8 on the wrong operator costs 0.2 to 0.5 expected successes over flat Thompson, strength 16 costs up to 1.1, and a right prior saves 0.9 to 2.4; a 50/50 mix of right and wrong still beats flat.
agent_test: Start each operator with 2 to 8 pseudo-counts from past tasks; compare with flat Beta(1,1) and with a deliberately wrong prior on logged runs.

claim: At a few dozen pulls, plain Thompson sampling needs no window or discount: published window and discount studies start at 200 pulls, the theoretical window sqrt(T ln T) is about a third of a 30-pull run, and in my simulation caps C=5 to 50 changed regret by under 0.15 at T=30 and 60, with or without a mid-run switch.
agent_test: Compare plain Thompson with a cap of 20 on logged runs of 40 or more pulls; keep plain if no gain.

claim: For picking one final candidate at about 5 evaluations each, simulated successive halving, tuned UCB and Thompson sampling all beat uniform allocation by 1.1x to 2x in P(best) and are close to each other (halving within 0.03 to 0.04 of the best); halving beats plain UCB1 (c=1) only when candidates outnumber the budget (K=30). Original halving results (Jamieson and Talwalkar) concern converging training curves, not i.i.d. judgments. No ARC or BrainTeaser run exists.
agent_test: Replay ARC and BrainTeaser candidate sets with 5 checks each under halving, Thompson and uniform allocation.

claim: An LLM can serve as a bandit prior rather than the chooser: LLM-simulated users used to pre-train a contextual bandit cut cumulative regret by 14 to 17 percent (LLM oracle) and 19 to 20 percent (real conjoint data) at T=1000, with diminishing returns as real data arrives. It was not compared with LLM-as-chooser, with hand priors, or at small horizons.
agent_test: Ask the model for per-operator pseudo-counts, cap at 4 to 8, compare with flat prior and with the model choosing.

claim: No source compares a state-keyed operator bandit with a global one at small budgets. The best data point is a hand-built 4-state weight table with relative-improvement credit in Deliberate Evolution (uniform sampling 23x worse in NMSE, fixed refine 20x worse, run count not stated). Contextual Thompson guarantees are vacuous below T = d^3, and 30 pulls over several states leaves about 3 to 10 per state, so any state-keying needs pooling toward a global mean or a hand-set prior.
agent_test: Replay logs with a 3-state key (early, mid, late parent quality) pooled toward a global mean versus a global bandit.
